title: Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
claim: Date-restricted searches still surface content that leaks future knowledge, so retrieval-based evaluations are contaminated in ways that are hard to filter.
layout: 2 panels side by side, screenshots with captions underneath, reading left-to-right
description: Two side-by-side screenshots of web search results, each with a caption beneath. Panel (a) is a Google search for "jan 6" with a date filter of 1 Jan 2015 to 31 Dec 2019. It lists Britannica, House.gov and US Navy History results. The Britannica snippet is dated 2017 but describes the 2021 Capitol attack, so it leaks future information. Panel (b) is a DuckDuckGo search for "wuhan" restricted to 1 Jan 2016 to 31 Dec 2018. It shows a YouTube video and a Scientific American article about the Wuhan lab studying dangerous pathogens. Both panels use standard search-engine styling with blue link titles on white backgrounds. The eye lands first on the search bars and date filters, then on the highlighted results. The captions explain the leakage.
caption: Examples of hard-to-filter temporal leakage in search engines, bypassing date restrictions.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been applied to forecasting tasks, with some works claiming these systems match or exceed human performance. In this paper, we argue that, as a community, we should be careful about such conclusions as evaluating LLM forecasters presents unique challenges. We identify two broad categories of issues: (1) difficulty in trusting evaluation results due to many forms of temporal leakage, and (2) difficulty in extrapolating from evaluation performance to real-world forecasting. Through systematic analysis and concrete examples from prior work, we demonstrate how evaluation flaws can raise concerns about current and future performance claims. We argue that more rigorous evaluation methodologies are needed to confidently assess the forecasting abilities of LLMs.
